questions.question: Why is simplicity important when choosing an algorithm for long-term use?
gold_points: A simple algorithm is easier to implement correctly than a complex one.
It is less likely to contain subtle bugs that appear later on unexpected inputs.
A simple algorithm is also easier for other people to understand and maintain over time.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: How can good documentation help when an algorithm is not very simple?
gold_points: Good comments and documentation can partially compensate for a lack of simplicity.
Clear explanations make the algorithm easier for a reasonably intelligent reader to understand.
Better documentation helps later modification and maintenance by other programmers.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: Why can a linear-time algorithm become preferable to a quadratic-time algorithm as input size grows?
gold_points: A quadratic-time algorithm can be faster on small inputs because of constant factors.
As input size increases, the slower growth rate of a linear-time algorithm gives it an increasing advantage.
The functional form of the running time ultimately determines how large a problem the program can handle.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 6 (book page 94)
